1) Doubly robust DID estimators can be constructed for the average treatment on the treated (the effect of treatment on a subset of individuals that actually receive treatment), which have the desirable property of being consistent if either the propensity score or outcome model is correctly specified.

(1) we propose a class of doubly robust estimators of the ATT in DID research designs, (2) we show that these estimators are semiparametric efficient when the working models in these estimators are correctly specified, (3) we show that one may sometimes construct a doubly robust DID estimator of the ATT that also allows for doubly robust inference, (4) we show that having access to panel instead of cross section data can lead to efficiency gains in policy evaluation

(1) doubly robust estimators of the ATT in difference in differences research designs can be constructed, (2) these estimators are consistent under weaker assumptions than alternative estimators, (3) these estimators attain the efficiency bound under correct model specification, (4) the efficiency bound can be substantially larger for panel data than for repeated cross section data, and (5) one can sometimes construct confidence intervals for the ATT in difference-in-differences research designs that are robust to model misspecification

we provide the first set of estimators that are consistent for the average treatment effects on the treated in the difference in differences framework, when the working model for the outcome is not correctly specified, or the working model for propensity is not correctly specified.

The main takeaway from our work is that
, when one has access to panel data, doubly robust DID estimator can be used to estimate the ATT in DID research designs with minimal assumptions.

the ATT in DID research designs is often identifiable under weaker conditions than commonly thought, and that one can often construct efficient estimators for the same under weaker conditions than those required to construct efficient estimators of the average treatment effect in standard regression discontinuity designs.
, in the presence of a large number of covariates, doubly robust estimators are often preferable to standard estimators for the treatment effect of interest.
